intro: Only one of Belfast's oldest trees is an oak, and nobody has settled which oak it is. The Belvoir Oak, in a forest park in the south, is called the oldest living oak in Ireland by the department that manages the ground, though two veterans stand near the Motte and sources disagree about which carries the name. In the Botanic Gardens an Australian grass tree over 400 years old has lived under glass since Victoria's reign, beside a dawn redwood from the year the species came back from the fossil record. The fourth is a hawthorn that named a graveyard.
meta_description: Belfast's oldest trees: an oak called the oldest in Ireland, a 400-year-old Australian grass tree under glass, and a thorn that named a graveyard.
question_answer: The oldest tree in Belfast is the Belvoir Oak in Belvoir Park Forest, in the south of the city. DAERA, the government department that manages the forest, calls it the oldest living oak in Ireland at 500 to 600 years old; a senior ranger who assessed it in 2016 said more than 400 and that its condition makes an exact age impossible, so the honest band is 400 to 600. It stands near the Motte, roughly a 15 minute walk from Galwally halt, and the pin here marks the forest rather than the trunk.
question_meta: Belfast's oldest tree is the Belvoir Oak, put at 400 to 600 years. Which of two veteran oaks near the Motte carries the name is still unsettled.
question_context:
There is an unresolved question sitting under that answer, and it is worth knowing before the walk. Robert Welch photographed a great oak in Belvoir Park Forest more than a century ago, already well over 300 years old and known locally as Granddad. Northern Ireland's Remarkable Trees project states plainly that Granddad may not be the same specimen as the tree now promoted as the Belvoir Oak, which means two distinct veterans may stand near the Motte, one of them seriously declined and the other healthier and better publicised. Nobody has settled it in public, and a reader who walks that ground can probably settle it faster than we can.

One rival for the title is not an oak and not a tree. The Australian grass tree inside the Palm House at the Botanic Gardens is put at over 400 years, which overlaps the oak's range, and it is a monocot rather than a tree in the usual sense. On the numbers as they stand the oak takes it, on a range that runs from 400 years to 600.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Belfast?
faq.a: The Belvoir Oak in Belvoir Park Forest. DAERA calls it the oldest living oak in Ireland at 500 to 600 years; a 2016 ranger assessment says more than 400 and that the tree's condition makes an exact figure impossible. The honest band is 400 to 600.

faq.q: Are Belfast's oldest trees free to visit?
faq.a: All of them are free. Belvoir Park Forest is open around the clock, the Botanic Gardens and the Palm House cost nothing to enter, and Friar's Bush Graveyard is free too, though it is kept locked and you have to book a slot with Belfast City Council before you go.

faq.q: How do you get into Friar's Bush Graveyard?
faq.a: By arranging it first. Belfast City Council manages the site and admits visitors on a booked slot, by telephone on 028 9027 0296 or by email; Cairde na Cille and the Friends of Friar's Bush Graveyard also run guided tours. Turning up unannounced gets you a look at the wall.

faq.q: Is the grass tree in the Palm House really a tree?
faq.a: No. Xanthorrhoea preissii is an Australian monocot in the asphodel family, no closer to an oak than a lily is. It grows a dark trunk of packed old leaf bases, it is the oldest living thing in the Botanic Gardens, and it is worth the detour precisely because it is odd.

trees.name: The Belvoir Oak

location.address: Belvoir Park Forest, near the Motte, off the Outer Ring Road (A55) car park, Belfast BT8

trees.story:
In the winter of 2016 a ranger counted the acorns on this oak. There were six, and he called that remarkable, because the tree by then barely had enough branches and twigs left to make them. Dan Clarke, senior ranger for the Lagan Valley Regional Park, put it at more than 400 years old and said outright that its condition made an exact age impossible. He measured the girth at just under nine metres.

Other authorities go higher. DAERA, the department that manages the forest, calls it the oldest living oak in Ireland at 500 to 600 years, dating it to the 1500s, and fronted a photography exhibition with it here in 2023. The Ancient Tree Forum settles on about 500.

And then there is the question nobody has answered in public. Robert Welch photographed a great oak in this forest more than a century ago, already well over 300 years old and known locally as Granddad. Northern Ireland's Remarkable Trees project says Granddad may not be the tree now promoted as the Belvoir Oak, and that two distinct veterans may stand near the Motte, one failing and one healthier. We could not resolve which is which. If you walk this forest and know, tell us.

Whichever it is, the wood around it lost roughly a quarter of its trees to sudden oak death in 2014, and this one came through with the help of tree specialists.
trees.how_to_recognise: Two veteran oaks are reported near the Motte and sources disagree about which carries the name. Look for the vast hollow one, just under nine metres round, with very little live crown left.
trees.access: Free. Forest Service NI managed forest park, open 24 hours, car park off the Outer Ring Road (A55); also reachable via the Lagan towpath from Shaw's Bridge or the Galwally Avenue entrance.
trees.transport: Galwally rail halt (Lagan Valley line) approx 15 min walk; several Translink bus routes serve Outer Ring Road / Milltown Road nearby.
trees.notes: Species given only as 'oak' in every source; robur vs petraea not established. The ~880cm girth is from the 2016 Irish News report about 'Granddad'; if Granddad and the currently promoted 'Belvoir Oak' are two different trees, that girth may not belong to this individual. Pin is the forest/Motte area, not the trunk: Ancient Tree Forum gives grid ref J338696, which a future pass should convert properly or replace with a geotagged photo before upgrading precision.

trees.name: The Grass Tree of the Palm House

location.address: The Palm House, Belfast Botanic Gardens, College Gardens, Belfast BT9 6BQ

trees.story:
The oldest living thing in the Belfast Botanic Gardens is not a tree. Xanthorrhoea preissii is an Australian grass tree, a monocot in the asphodel family, no closer to an oak than a lily is, and it builds its dark trunk out of the packed bases of leaves it shed centuries ago. This one is reckoned to be over 400 years old, which puts its first growth somewhere around the reign of Elizabeth I.

It came to Belfast during Queen Victoria's reign and has spent every year since under cast iron and glass. The Palm House it stands in is older than most of the plants around it: foundation stone in 1839, the wings finished the following year, the dome added in 1852. A plant that predates the building by two centuries now depends on it entirely, because nothing in this climate would keep a Western Australian grass tree alive outdoors.

The hardest recent evidence that it is still standing is that it came through the Palm House's major renovation in 2005, when the glasshouse was stripped and rebuilt around its collection. Visitor guides written since describe it in the present tense, which is reassuring rather than conclusive. If you have seen it lately, better still photographed it, we would like to hear from you.
trees.access: Free entry to the gardens; the Palm House itself is open daily, 10am to 4pm April to September, 10am to 3:45pm October to March.
trees.transport: Botanic rail halt approx 5 min walk; several Metro/Glider bus routes stop on Botanic Avenue/University Road nearby.
trees.notes: Not a tree in the botanical sense; framed honestly in the story. Three sources agree on 'over 400 years' and arrival during Victoria's reign. Most concrete dated evidence of life is survival of the 2005 Palm House renovation; no dated 2020s sighting or photograph found, so the recency gap is stated in the prose. Pin is the Palm House building, not the individual bed inside it.

trees.name: The Dawn Redwood by the Kelvin Statue

location.address: Belfast Botanic Gardens, near the Kelvin statue by the Malone Road entrance, Belfast BT9

trees.story:
Until 1946 this species existed only as a fossil. Metasequoia was known from stone impressions and presumed extinct until living trees were found in China that year. Seed reached the Arnold Arboretum in Boston in 1948, and the seedlings raised from it were the first dawn redwoods sent out to botanic gardens around the world.

Belfast's came almost immediately. The Friends of Belfast Botanic Gardens date this specimen to about 1950, which makes it one of the first dawn redwoods grown in Ireland after the species came back. It carries tag number 59, and the Tree Council of Ireland's register lists it as a notable tree.

At roughly 76 years old it is young for a tree with a page here, and that is the interesting part: the whole cultivated stock outside China began with one sowing in Boston, and this is one of the first of those plants to reach the island. It is also a conifer that behaves like a broadleaf. The needles come through fresh green in spring, and in late October they turn rust orange and fall, the whole lot of them, which is not what a conifer is supposed to do.

Three dawn redwoods now grow in these gardens, which is a fair measure of how quickly a resurrected species can be made ordinary.
trees.how_to_recognise: Three dawn redwoods grow in these gardens. This is the one by the Kelvin statue; the other two stand in the rock garden and on the path from the Malone gate to the Palm House.
trees.access: Free. Belfast Botanic Gardens, open daily during daylight hours.
trees.transport: Botanic rail halt approx 5 min walk; several Metro/Glider bus routes stop on Botanic Avenue/University Road nearby.
trees.notes: Age estimated from the documented planting/distribution era for the species after its 1946 rediscovery, not from a girth measurement. A search summary claiming a 22m height from monumentaltrees.com was NOT verified on the page and is deliberately excluded. Two other Metasequoia specimens stand in the same gardens, which matters for any photo match.

best_time.label: late October into November, when the needles turn rust orange and drop, which is not what a conifer is supposed to do

trees.name: The Friar's Bush Hawthorn
trees.age_estimate: not documented; described as old and reclining

location.address: Friar's Bush Graveyard, Stranmillis Road, Belfast BT9, beside the Ulster Museum

trees.story:
Belfast's oldest Christian burial ground is named after this hawthorn. Under the Penal Laws of the eighteenth century, when the Mass was banned, Catholics gathered in secret beneath a thorn on this ground to hear it said. Belfast City Council and Northern Ireland's Remarkable Trees project tell it the same way, and the name stuck: Friar's Bush. The poet Joseph Campbell called it the Stranmillis trysting thorn. A darker version of the legend has a friar murdered and buried by the spot where he preached, with a stone laid over the grave.

The tree itself is low and undramatic, reclining rather than standing, in the middle of the graveyard. Nobody has dated it and nobody has put a tape round it. Remarkable Trees puts the impression well: it may well bow down under the weight of its history. If you know an age or a girth for it, tell us, because we do not.

Getting in takes a phone call. The graveyard is kept locked and Belfast City Council admits visitors on a booked slot, on 028 9027 0296 or by email, and guided tours run through Cairde na Cille and the Friends of Friar's Bush Graveyard. It costs nothing, there is no parking on site, and some paths are not passable in a wheelchair. Turning up unannounced gets you a look at the wall.
trees.how_to_recognise: The low, leaning hawthorn in the middle of the graveyard, spreading rather than tall.
trees.access: Free, but not walk-up: the graveyard is kept locked and Belfast City Council admits visitors on a booked slot (telephone 028 9027 0296 or email the council); Cairde na Cille and the Friends of Friar's Bush Graveyard also run guided tours. No car parking on site; some paths are unsuitable for wheelchairs.
trees.transport: Metro 8A-B from Belfast city centre, alight at Botanic Gardens; Botanic rail halt also nearby.
trees.notes: No numeric age or girth found anywhere; described only as old and reclining. Council's page places it in the centre of the cemetery, hence the park-level pin. No dated 2020s sighting of the specific tree found, though the site is actively managed and toured. Access is bookable and free, which is the 2026-09-01 ruling's price-and-schedule case rather than somebody's permission.

best_time.label: May, when a hawthorn turns white all over and the whole graveyard smells of it
